title: The white bear
hookLine: told not to think of a white bear, people thought of it more (Wegner)

lines: DON'T THINK OF A WHITE BEAR.
WEGNER TAKES IT TO THE LAB.
cards: A small experiment, right now. For the next five seconds, do not think about a white bear. Not a polar bear on the ice.
Not a white bear in the snow. No bear of any kind. How did that go?
The Russian novelist Fyodor Dostoevsky set this little challenge in an essay, and said the bear would come to mind every minute.
Much later, a psychologist named Daniel Wegner read that line and decided to test it in a lab. The bear is today's word.

teach.h: RING THE BELL FOR EVERY BEAR.
teach.b: First, the experiment. Wegner and his colleagues asked people to think aloud for a few minutes while trying not to think of a white bear, and to ring a bell whenever it came to mind. They rang it again and again.
Second, the rebound. Afterward, people were told they could now think about the bear freely.

teach.h: PUSHED AWAY, IT CAME BACK MORE.
teach.b: Those who had first tried to push it away thought about it more than people who had been allowed to think about it from the start. Suppressing the thought seemed to keep it close.
Wegner later offered an explanation: to check that you're not thinking of the bear, part of the mind has to keep looking for the bear. Third, what helped.

In another version, people were given something else to think of whenever the bear turned up: a red Volkswagen. With a replacement ready, the rebound shrank. Fourth, an old teaching that lands in the same place.

teach.h: A FINE PEG DRIVES OUT A COARSE ONE.
teach.b: In a discourse from the Buddhist Middle Length Sayings, the Buddha describes a carpenter knocking out a coarse peg by driving in a finer one.
When an unhelpful thought keeps returning, the instruction is to bring in a skillful one in its place. Not 'stop thinking that.' Think this instead.
A thought leaves more easily when something else is ready to take its seat.

how: Meditation teachers and therapists who use this research often suggest giving the mind a chosen place to go, such as the breath, when a thought returns, rather than trying to push the thought away.

o: a thought that vanishes once you push it away hard
a rare animal from a well-known Russian novel
a thought you try not to think, which keeps coming back

games.q: inside the white bear: tap the pairs.
p: took the bear to the lab
a fine peg for a coarse one

s: trying hard not to think of something makes it go away
in Wegner's study, people kept ringing the bell for the bear.
after suppressing the bear, people later thought of it more
the rebound: they thought of it more than people allowed to think of it from the start.
the Buddhist teaching says simply to stop the thought
the carpenter swaps a coarse peg for a finer one: replace, don't just push out.

games.q: you're in Wegner's study and the bear keeps coming back. which instruction made the rebound shrink?
o: try even harder not to think of it.
think of a red Volkswagen whenever it comes.
games.why: with a replacement thought ready, the rebound shrank. pushing harder is what kept the bear close.

practice: Before the sit, name a thought that keeps coming back, a worry, an old argument, a list, and choose its replacement: the feeling of air at the nostrils.
When the thought returns, don't shove it out; say 'peg' silently and set the breath in its place. Again and again, gently, as often as it takes.

wordCard.voice: The white bear. Trying hard not to think a thought can keep it close; giving the mind something else to hold works better. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: not the bear. Think of this, instead of trying not to think of that. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Wegner, Schneider, Carter & White, "Paradoxical effects of thought suppression"
